title: Any Time, Any Space: A World-State-Centric Framework for Agentic Video Generation

details.title: Any Time, Any Space: A World-State-Centric Framework for Agentic Video Generation
details.abstract: Excited to share ATAS — Any Time, Any Space ! Video models can produce impressive individual shots, but keeping a whole story consistent is harder: a room should keep its layout when revisited, and different cameras should capture the same event at the same point in time. We introduce ATAS , a world-state-centric framework that gives video agents a shared spatial and temporal reference. 🧠 Two complementary memories : scene memory stores registered static geometry, while event memory stores time-indexed dynamic observations. Each new shot retrieves the evidence it needs. 🎥 Different cameras, one event : agents can revisit earlier locations or replay past events from new viewpoints, querying the same evolving world state. 📊 Evaluated across four video generators : ATAS improves the reported cross-shot consistency measures, with further evaluations covering spatial revisits, event recapture, and human preferences. Any Time, Any Space. Every shot has a history. 🌐 Project page & interactive demo 💻 Code 🎬 Promo video Try the demo to explore the point clouds, camera poses, and linked videos!

title: Recovering Reliable Supervision via Critique-Guided On-Policy Distillation

details.title: Recovering Reliable Supervision via Critique-Guided On-Policy Distillation
details.abstract: 🤖 CriticOPD: Recovering Reliable Supervision via Critique-Guided On-Policy Distillation 🔍 Key finding: Teachers can recognize student mistakes yet still follow them when continuing a flawed solution, making OPD supervision unreliable. ✍️ Our approach: The teacher uses the reference answer to critique incorrect student rollouts, and the student rewrites the continuation with this feedback. The teacher scores the rewritten suffix with the feedback in context, while the student learns from that suffix without seeing the feedback. 📈 Results: Across six math reasoning benchmarks, CriticOPD improves average accuracy over OPD by 4.57 percentage points on Qwen3-1.7B and 4.06 on Qwen3-0.6B , with the largest gains on competition problems. 🌐 Project page · 💻 Code

title: Doc2Harness: Benchmarking LLMs on Long-Horizon Harness Engineering of Coding Agents

details.title: Doc2Harness: Benchmarking LLMs on Long-Horizon Harness Engineering of Coding Agents
details.abstract: Agents driven by large language models are increasingly deployed on long-horizon tasks, where they use tools and modify real workspaces. How well they perform depends as much on the harness around the model as on the model itself. Existing benchmarks measure downstream task success under a fixed harness, leaving harness engineering itself unexplored. We propose Doc2Harness, a two-stage benchmark that evaluates long-horizon harness engineering directly. In Stage 1, a build model operating inside a fixed builder harness receives an interface-only contract skeleton and a development document that consolidates behavior across twelve frontier harnesses, and then constructs a complete candidate harness in an isolated container. In Stage 2, the frozen candidate harness runs in containers separate from the construction environment, one per test case, and is driven end to end by a scripted mock model. We score each test case using four observable channels, namely the requests sent to the model, the files on disk, the process exit code, and the command output; positive controls rule out vacuous passes. Across nineteen frontier models, each evaluated with three independent builds on 328 test cases, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest pass rate at 53.05%, while the weakest model reaches 27.44%, a gap of roughly twenty-six percentage points. Even the strongest model fails nearly half of the test cases, and failures cluster around how cross-cutting functionality is split across modules. To our knowledge, Doc2Harness provides the first deterministic benchmark for measuring long-horizon harness engineering.

title: Beyond Domain-Routed Supervision: Cross-Teacher Guarding for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation

details.title: Beyond Domain-Routed Supervision: Cross-Teacher Guarding for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
details.abstract: Developed jointly by JD.com’s OxygenVLM team and Nanjing University, RoadMOPD mitigates learning conflicts among teachers with substantially different response styles and domain expertise, helping a student integrate multiple experts’ capabilities while reducing degradation in individual domains. It brings routed and auxiliary teachers together to evaluate the same student-generated response, using teacher agreement to strengthen jointly supported token-level corrections and attenuate conflicting signals. Preventive gradient projection then suppresses conflicting update components while adaptively preserving the target domain’s learning signal. With Qwen3-4B, RoadMOPD improves both domains over Vanilla MOPD in the high-conflict Math–Medical and Code–Medical settings, boosting average medical accuracy by up to 8.78 percentage points. Benefits also extend to the more compatible Math–Code combination, with improvements across all three domains under joint Math–Code–Medical training. The code is currently undergoing internal company approval for open-source release and is expected to be released within the next 1–2 months.

title: Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning: The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory

details.title: Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning: The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory
details.abstract: How can multimodal agents remember what they perceive, keep that memory useful as the world changes, and learn to manage it better over time? We are sharing our survey, “Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning: The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory.” We organize this growing field around two complementary axes: 🔹 Formation and Representation: How is multimodal information stored—as modality-specific representations, text and structured records, latent or parametric memory, or hybrid representations that preserve links to the original evidence? 🔹 Memory Management: How does memory adapt over time? We distinguish static memory , dynamic memory updated through a stable policy, and self-evolving memory whose management policy improves through experience. A central distinction is that updating memory content and improving the policy that manages memory are different capabilities . Our framework helps clarify this difference and connects memory design to evidence preservation, temporal consistency, and reliable reasoning across long-horizon tasks. The survey also covers memory infrastructure, evaluation benchmarks, applications, and open challenges. We hope it serves as a useful guide for researchers and practitioners building multimodal agents. We welcome feedback, discussion, and suggestions for relevant work!

title: More Methods, Better Agents? A Reality Check on Self-Distillation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning

details.title: More Methods, Better Agents? A Reality Check on Self-Distillation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
details.abstract: We present a large-scale, systematic evaluation of self-distillation methods in agentic reinforcement learning, revealing that existing methods struggle to consistently outperform GRPO despite increased computational costs. We hope our work provides the community with a fair and reliable benchmark, encouraging future research toward more robust, stable, and cost-effective agent training.

title: KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization

details.title: KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization
details.abstract: Excited to share KV4-RL! We investigate KV cache quantization for accelerating asynchronous RLVR rollouts. Our key finding is that asynchronous scheduling makes KV cache a major performance bottleneck, while aggressive INT4 quantization can compromise learning stability. KV4-RL combines calibration-free INT4 KV quantization with selective INT8 protection, delivering up to 1.97× rollout speedup and 1.27× end-to-end speedup, with minimal impact on learning performance. Feedback and discussions are very welcome!

title: APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation

details.title: APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation
details.abstract: Better models. Smarter training data. Different image models struggle with different things. A fixed training set cannot keep up with every model’s evolving strengths and weaknesses. APT makes post-training adaptive. Three agents work together to evaluate the current model, diagnose its failure modes, and generate the training prompts it needs next. After each update, the loop starts again. APT (Agentic Post-Training) turns post-training into a fully automated, evaluation-driven adaptive loop. Given a user-specified evaluation scope, the Evaluation Set Generation Agent constructs a diverse evaluation set consisting of prompt–evaluation rubric pairs; the Diagnosis Agent evaluates the current model on these pairs to identify its strengths and failure modes; and the RL Data Generation Agent adaptively samples next-round training prompts, prioritizing underperforming capabilities. The updated model is then re-evaluated in the next round, allowing the training distribution to continuously adapt to the model's evolving capability profile. This design eliminates the need for manually curated post-training data and makes APT model-agnostic, benchmark-agnostic, architecture-agnostic, and fully automated.

title: HumanoidToolBench: Benchmarking Humanoid Tool Use from Selection to Mobile Execution

details.title: HumanoidToolBench: Benchmarking Humanoid Tool Use from Selection to Mobile Execution
details.abstract: Can humanoids choose the right tool and then actually use it? We introduce HumanoidToolBench, an 18-task benchmark evaluating humanoid tool selection and execution across three scenarios, three execution levels, and two tool-set modes. We also introduce ToolBook, a dataset of 3.1k demonstrations collected in simulation and on a real Unitree G1. Evaluating seven policies in simulation and three on the real robot reveals a substantial gap between selecting a suitable tool and successfully completing the task. Additional GR00T N1.7 probes examine generalization to unseen tools and behavior under unrelated instructions. Explore the benchmark and demonstrations on our project page. We welcome feedback from the humanoid learning and tool-use communities!

title: RuleTrek: Benchmarking Agentic Rule Reasoning in Complex Scenarios

details.title: RuleTrek: Benchmarking Agentic Rule Reasoning in Complex Scenarios
details.abstract: RuleTrek is a multi-domain benchmark for evaluating agentic rule reasoning in complex scenarios. Unlike existing rule-reasoning benchmarks that represent scenarios using only a few factual statements, RuleTrek features complex, multi-file scenarios that require agents to integrate distributed information, identify applicable rules from original rule documents, and correctly apply them to solve tasks in interactive workspaces. RuleTrek evaluates three core capabilities: Rule Identification (RI), Rule Deduction (RD), and End-to-End Rule Reasoning (E2E). Experiments on 11 frontier LLMs reveal substantial challenges, with E2E scores ranging from 26.97% to 55.29%.

title: τ-Emotion-Bench: Exposing the Interaction Fragility of LLM Agents through Real-World User Emotions

details.title: τ-Emotion-Bench: Exposing the Interaction Fragility of LLM Agents through Real-World User Emotions
details.abstract: In long-horizon tool-calling tasks, LLM agents can fail not only because of tool-use errors, but also because of ineffective interaction with users. Yet existing benchmarks largely assume cooperative and behaviorally stable users, leaving the effect of emotional variation on agent reliability underexplored. We introduce τ-Emotion-Bench, a ten-domain benchmark for evaluating tool-calling agents under controlled emotion-conditioned user interactions while preserving the underlying task objective. To scale both benchmark construction and agent training, we introduce Tracer, a scalable agentic data-generation pipeline that constructs grounded, policy-valid tasks and collects trajectories through an interactive agent–user–environment harness. By allowing dissatisfied users to terminate inefficient interactions, the harness provides an interaction-aware signal that filters trajectories with excessive user dependence and favors effective tool use. Experiments with two user simulators show that frontier agents remain unreliable, with substantial gaps between average task success and consistent task completion. Tracer-generated supervision consistently improves Qwen3 models across scales, generalizes to unseen domains, and transfers to τ-Bench and τ-Trait. Behavioral analyses further show that higher task success is associated with a better balance between tool execution and necessary user follow-up. Overall, τ-Emotion-Bench and Tracer provide a scalable framework for evaluating agent reliability under diverse user behaviors and improving tool-calling agents through interaction-aware supervision.

title: RAR: Rate-Adaptive Rollout for Time-Consistent Interactive World Models

details.title: RAR: Rate-Adaptive Rollout for Time-Consistent Interactive World Models
details.abstract: Hi everyone! We’re sharing RAR (Rate-Adaptive Rollout), a framework for controllable generation rates in interactive world models. Most world models run at a fixed temporal rate, so differences in hardware throughput can unintentionally speed up or slow down the generated world. RAR combines physical-time-aligned Stride-RoPE with synchronized multi-stride training, enabling one model to generate at multiple rates—including unseen intermediate rates—and switch rates mid-rollout without resetting the KV cache. This makes it possible to match the rollout rate to runtime throughput while keeping the world’s physical-time progression consistent. Happy to discuss and hear your feedback!

title: SwarmRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Scientific Agent Swarm

details.title: SwarmRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Scientific Agent Swarm
details.abstract: Something I keep noticing with AI scientist agents: running more of them in parallel doesn’t make them smarter by default. Mostly they throw away each other’s work. 🧪 Picture a lab where a student has a promising idea but botches the implementation, and the idea gets crossed off. Down the hall, another student’s “failed” project holds the one trick a colleague needed, and nobody ever opens it. Agent swarms run into the same two walls: • A failed experiment doesn’t tell you whether the hypothesis was wrong or the code was • A program with no overall gain can still hold a component another agent needs • So good ideas get abandoned and useful pieces get buried That’s the problem behind our new paper: 🚀 SwarmRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Scientific Agent Swarm The idea: let the swarm evolve what its agents inherit, not just keep its best scores. • A shared graph records each research state: hypotheses, programs, experimental evidence and open needs • Feedback-Guided Swarm Mutation uses other agents’ feedback to decide whether to revise the hypothesis or repair the program • Complementary Swarm Recombination re-tests kept hypotheses on other agents’ programs (rebase) and merges components that complement each other (crossover) • Recursive Swarm Evolution sends every outcome back into the graph, whether it succeeded, failed or made no gain, so it shapes where the next agent starts Results on 118 scientific coding and ML engineering tasks: 📈 76.2 average on OpenProblems (single-cell), vs 57.2 for human experts and 67.1 for TusoAI 🧬 Matches published SOTA on 44.4% of NatureBench’s 90 tasks, the highest of all compared methods (the best Claude Code setup reaches 35.6%) 🏅 Medals on 81.8% of MLE-Bench Lite competitions, above Arbor and MLEvolve 🔁 About 77% of final best NatureBench programs come from a rebase, a crossover or a feedback-triggered update 🔬 Biologists reproduced two of its programs and used them in follow-up studies of intestinal and splenic immunity I think the next progress in AI for science will come less from adding agents or scaling models, and more from making sure what one agent learns changes where the next one begins. 📝 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20431

title: GroundGUI: GUI Grounding by High-Quality Data and Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning

details.title: GroundGUI: GUI Grounding by High-Quality Data and Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning
details.abstract: ScreenRef and Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning (D2RL) are the core contributions of GroundGUI. ScreenRef is a high-quality GUI grounding dataset spanning desktop, web, and mobile environments. It pairs diverse screenshots with referring expressions and localization annotations, covering text recognition, visual matching, spatial understanding, and refusal. Building on ScreenRef, we train GroundGUI-8B from Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct with supervised fine-tuning and D2RL, improving precise localization in complex interfaces.

title: Efficient Scene-Text Refinement via Pixel-Space Grouped Image Generation

details.title: Efficient Scene-Text Refinement via Pixel-Space Grouped Image Generation
details.abstract: 🚀 Great image, garbled text? Meet PixText, our approach to precise and efficient scene-text refinement. By generating only the target regions directly in pixel space, PixText corrects small text and complex characters while preserving the surrounding image. On our new Text Refinement Bench, it achieves 94.66% exact target-character OCR accuracy, compared with 52.31% for the strongest baseline. For fast inference, our four-step MeanFlow variant retains an 81.84% glyph pass rate at less than one GPU-second per image in amortized generation cost. We’re excited to share this step toward making generated images more readable and usable—feedback is welcome! 🤗

title: SafeDriveVLA: Navigation-Conditioned World Model Dreaming for Conflict-Aware End-to-End Autonomous Driving

details.title: SafeDriveVLA: Navigation-Conditioned World Model Dreaming for Conflict-Aware End-to-End Autonomous Driving
details.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are gaining attention in autonomous driving, inheriting commonsense priors from large language models (LLMs) and widening the navigation interface from a fixed command set to free-form natural-language instructions. However, this open-ended interface exposes a new vulnerability surface: an inattentive driver may issue instructions that are unsafe given the current scene, and a malicious user may issue dangerous ones on purpose. We present the first benchmark suite that evaluates navigation following and conflict awareness together, along with adversarial robustness. Existing VLAs fall short on both: SimLingo completes no language-instructed lane change in closed loop, and all models degrade sharply under conflicting signals. We propose SafeDriveVLA, the first driving VLA that (1) explicitly predicts a three-level navigation-compliance mode to decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and (2) uses navigation-conditioned world model dreaming to inform this prediction. Unlike prior world models that roll out expert or planned actions, ours dreams of strictly following the navigation signal, showing when following is safe. SafeDriveVLA reaches 88.16 Driving Score (DS) and 68.64% Success Rate (SR) on Bench2Drive, lifts closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 compared to the best SimLingo variant.

title: Long-Horizon RL Needs Muon

details.title: Long-Horizon RL Needs Muon
details.abstract: Long-horizon agents must coordinate reasoning, tool use, and environment feedback over extended interactions. Learning from sparse outcome rewards requires weighting trajectories of different lengths and updating the policy while rollouts are still being collected. We examine a single-rollout asynchronous recipe combining Muon , token-averaged loss, truncated importance sampling, and auxiliary length and tool-error penalties. Single-rollout sampling allows asynchronous learning without waiting for multiple trajectories for the same issue. We study optimizer choices and recipe components for repository-level issue resolution across two model families. The evaluated training runs show higher training success with the full recipe than with the baselines.

title: Acting Through Registers

details.title: Acting Through Registers
details.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) use generative visual representations to condition robot actions, yet how these representations organize action-relevant information remains poorly understood. We identify persistent high-norm spatial outliers in WAM representations and find that their action relevance persists even after normalization and K/V projection attenuate their extreme magnitude. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RegisterWAM, which adds learnable non-spatial registers to the world model and uses them directly for action conditioning. Registers alone do not fully eliminate spatial outliers; pairing them with observation flow-matching (FM) loss supervision suppresses spatial outliers while concentrating high-norm responses in registers. Beyond this reorganization, observation FM loss supervision also improves action learning without registers, motivating an additional noised-observation FM objective that learns current-scene recovery from corrupted inputs. The resulting model achieves 81.64% success on LIBERO-Plus without additional embodied pretraining data or foundation models, reaches 93.0% average success on RoboTwin 2.0, and improves real-world manipulation performance.

title: VITAL: From Visual Motion to Precise Action

details.title: VITAL: From Visual Motion to Precise Action
details.abstract: World-action models aim to turn visual anticipation into driving decisions, yet typically train action experts on trajectory representations defined independently of visual dynamics. This motivates deriving action targets directly from visual motion. We first examine a simpler setting in which trajectories are reconstructed from recorded future images. Even without the need for future prediction, reconstruction captures the dominant maneuver but leaves centimeter-scale errors. We therefore introduce VITAL (Vision-Induced Tokens for Action Learning), an action tokenizer that couples a visually derived motion scaffold with a compact residual encoding the trajectory error left by that scaffold. This representation makes visual motion the principal prediction target and gives small metric corrections a separate, normalized learning scale. Using flow matching, the action expert jointly predicts both components from the current image, ego state, and navigation command, without generating future images at inference. The same residual coordinates support bounded reinforcement post-training that refines execution while keeping the predicted visual scaffold fixed. With only one action denoising step, VITAL achieves 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, within 0.13 points of its ten-step score at 3.29x the end-to-end inference speed. Without retraining, it achieves 91.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and 38.6 on navhard.

title: TextVerifier: Seeing Beyond Recognition to Verify Chinese Text Rendering

details.title: TextVerifier: Seeing Beyond Recognition to Verify Chinese Text Rendering
details.abstract: 🔍 Readable doesn’t always mean correctly rendered. Meet TextVerifier, our model for detecting subtle errors in generated Chinese text—from missing strokes to malformed components—that OCR and vision-language models can overlook. By representing characters through Ideographic Description Sequences (IDS), TextVerifier learns to assess their visual structure. We also introduce TextRenderBench-ZH, a benchmark with 7,358 individually annotated characters, where TextVerifier achieves 0.844 F1, outperforming OCR confidence (0.526), a general VLM (0.329), and TextPecker (0.590). Beyond evaluation, its scores serve as per-character rewards for Flow-GRPO post-training, helping reduce rendering errors. We’re excited to share this step toward more reliable Chinese text generation—feedback is welcome! 🤗

title: LLM-to-Flow Distillation: Teaching Natural Language Goals to Scientific Generators

details.title: LLM-to-Flow Distillation: Teaching Natural Language Goals to Scientific Generators
details.abstract: We’re bringing natural-language control to any scientific generator. We are very excited to introduce LLM-to-Flow Distillation (LFD), a method to adapt scientific generators to high-level natural-language discovery goals. Starting from textual goals like “design peptides with promising anticancer activity” or “design small molecules binding to the D2 dopamine receptor”, LFD distills high-level goal-related knowledge from LLMs into scientific generators through iterative DPO on LLM-generated subgoals. 🔥 LFD does not need task-specific proxy rewards, works with any frontier LLM via API-access, and outperforms state-of-the-art reward-guided methods such as FlowGRPO and DiffusionNFT on held-out computational evaluations. Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17246 Website: https://llm-to-flow-distillation.github.io Code: https://github.com/FedericoDiGennaro/LLM-to-Flow-Distillation

title: Glance Forcing: Making Bidirectional Diffusion Autoregressive at a Glance

details.title: Glance Forcing: Making Bidirectional Diffusion Autoregressive at a Glance
details.abstract: we propose Glance Forcing, a lightweight distillation framework that decouples the denoising trajectory into two complementary slow and fast experts, each guided by a tailored, stage-specific objective. This decoupling further reveals a general mechanism underlying few-step distillation: PF-ODE distillation mainly straightens the few-step trajectory geometry, while the subsequent distribution-matching stage independently governs distributional quality.

title: What Makes a Social Agent's Interactions Effective? Learning from Verifiable Outcomes in Paired Worlds

details.title: What Makes a Social Agent's Interactions Effective? Learning from Verifiable Outcomes in Paired Worlds
details.abstract: Effective social interaction requires more than fluent responses: agents must reach plans that fit the participants' needs and circumstances. Existing evaluations of social agents mainly rely on LLM judges that rate the conversation, without checking the resulting plan. We introduce HICO-Bench, a benchmark of 180 everyday coordination scenarios, such as resource allocation, scheduling, and authorization, in which two agents with private information converse and then independently record the plan they agreed on. A program checks Feasibility (the two records match and satisfy both participants' private conditions), and an LLM judge checks Integrity (the conversation supports the recorded plan); passing both is a Verified Success. Each scenario has two versions that share the same public context but differ in one private condition, so the correct plan differs between them. Across thirteen LLMs, 36% of conversations rated highly for goal completion fail Verified Success. To learn from outcomes that arrive only at the end of a conversation, we propose Paired-Credit Policy Optimization (PaCPO). After each turn, PaCPO asks the agent for a tentative plan, checks it in both versions of the scenario, and rewards the turns after which the tentative plans fit their respective versions. PaCPO raises Qwen3-8B's Verified Success from 20.4% to 28.3%.

title: Physical Time as a Missing Dimension of Robot Policy Memory Dynamics

details.title: Physical Time as a Missing Dimension of Robot Policy Memory Dynamics
details.abstract: Robot policies act in physical time, but their memories are often organized around observation steps. What happens when these two clocks disagree? The same observation history can require different actions depending on how much time has elapsed. A robot making tea may see an unchanged scene, yet need to switch from waiting to lifting. The same observed displacement can imply different velocities, changing how a robot should intercept an object after it disappears from view. Remembering what happened is only part of the challenge; a policy must also determine what that history means now. We introduce Temporal Flow Policy (TFP), which makes physical time part of policy memory dynamics. Current observations and retained history shape each memory transition, while measured elapsed time determines how far the state advances. The resulting memory guides diffusion and flow-matching policies through their native imitation objectives. Through controlled comparisons, interventions on the supplied clock, and real-robot experiments, we investigate how retained history and physical time jointly shape behavior. TFP explores a broader design principle for robot learning: the internal state used for action should reflect both the history of observations and the physical time over which that history unfolds.

title: Exploring the Limits of Combinatorial Generalization in Embodied Manipulation

details.title: Exploring the Limits of Combinatorial Generalization in Embodied Manipulation
details.abstract: In embodied manipulation, Vision Language Action (VLA) models can execute atomic skills, but long-horizon manipulation requires recombining these skills without demonstrations for every skill combination. The full instruction route treats skill chaining as long-horizon imitation. In a controlled study, full instruction training on limited skill combination sequences reaches 40.0% ordered success on covered combinations but only 7.7% on recombination, suggesting memorization of sequence templates rather than robust skill recombination. We introduce Hierarchical Subtask Execution (HSE), a diagnostic framework that exposes skill recombination through a shared modular interface over the planner, trigger, and policy, decomposing long-horizon failures into separable modes. We introduce RoboCombine, a benchmark for skill recombination without combined skill training trajectories, with metrics for ordered success and transition conversion across subtask boundaries. RoboCombine reveals that atomic competence alone does not ensure ordered execution. Failures concentrate at transitions where downstream subtasks launch from handoff states from preceding subtasks rather than canonical atomic starts. We identify this mismatch as the start state gap. To address it, we introduce Pose Robust Task Initialization (PRTI), a lightweight atomic task post-training strategy that broadens start state coverage beyond canonical starts. Under oracle timed HSE on RoboCombine, PRTI reaches 18.16% ordered success, compared with 4.21% under random perturbation and 9.47% under a robot-reset oracle, without combined skill training trajectories. These results show that combinatorial generalization requires handoff robust atomic skills that convert first stage progress into reliable downstream execution, not merely decomposition into known subtasks.

title: DecisionRobust: Benchmarking Robustness for JEV Style Decision Models Across Text and Vision

details.title: DecisionRobust: Benchmarking Robustness for JEV Style Decision Models Across Text and Vision
details.abstract: We introduce DecisionRobust, a benchmark for testing the robustness of JEV-style decision models across text and vision, including classification, routing, tool selection, and robotics scenarios. Our public release contains 1,058 curated attack examples across five suites: meaning-preserving text attacks, text prompt injection, image perturbations, in-image instruction overlays, and instruction injection alongside images. We evaluate 30 model configurations on text and 17 on vision. One finding we found particularly interesting: resistance to input perturbations does not necessarily imply resistance to prompt injection. We also find that checking whether attacks preserve the correct answer substantially changes measured attack success. These are curated challenge sets, so the results should not be interpreted as real-world failure rates. 📊 Interactive leaderboard & examples ( https://yifan-lan.github.io/DecisionRobust/ ) 🤗 Dataset ( https://huggingface.co/datasets/yflantmy/DecisionRobust ) If you use decision models in an application, which failure mode would you most want a robustness benchmark to capture? We’d love suggestions for additional models and scenarios!

title: Continuum Attention

details.title: Continuum Attention
details.abstract: We introduce Continuum Attention (CA), a causal Transformer attention operator that replaces discrete key and value lookup with integration over a continuous, piecewise linear memory curve.

title: StartLux-Decision: AutoThink Decision Models with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions

details.title: StartLux-Decision: AutoThink Decision Models with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions
details.abstract: We introduce StartLux-Decision, decision models from 0.8B to 27B parameters that combine efficient single-pass prediction with adaptive, confidence-guided reasoning. The Instant models use bidirectional attention in full-attention layers to improve decision accuracy while keeping single-pass inference. The AutoThink models invoke explicit reasoning for uncertain decisions and answer confident cases directly. A three-stage training pipeline establishes shared decision capabilities, specializes the two variants, and equips AutoThink with reasoning through reasoning supervision and reinforcement learning. We introduce Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions (RLCD²), which uses a frozen model and proper scoring rules to reward improvements in decision probability quality and applies a soft penalty to overlong reasoning traces. RLCD² raises the share of reasoning traces that terminate within the generation limit by up to 48 percentage points and cuts average reasoning length by up to 65%, while largely preserving decision accuracy. On the public subset of Decision Index 0.3, the Instant models outperform the strongest evaluated comparable-scale open-weight decision models by 7.4–16.9 points, and the 27B AutoThink model reaches 73.4. We also introduce DecisionPivot, a programmatically verifiable benchmark of computational decisions built from contrast pairs that differ in a single answer-changing detail. On DecisionPivot, AutoThink outperforms its Instant counterparts by 11.5–18.4 points in pair accuracy and leads among evaluated systems. The models run on vLLM, llama.cpp and MLX, with quantized variants for lower memory use.

title: ProbabilityBench: Model Evaluation and Calibration with Exact Ground-Truth Uncertainty

details.title: ProbabilityBench: Model Evaluation and Calibration with Exact Ground-Truth Uncertainty
details.abstract: Decision models like Jev are designed to predict class probabilities directly, but how can we tell whether their predictions are actually correct? Suppose a decision model predicts a 70% probability that an instance belongs to the positive class in a binary classification task. Even after observing the true binary label, we still don’t know whether 70% was the right probability. Standard calibration metrics don’t fully answer this question either, because they evaluate predictions in aggregate rather than for individual instances. Proper scoring rules such as log loss are useful for evaluating probabilistic predictions, but without knowing the irreducible loss, we cannot determine how much of the observed loss comes from inaccurate probability estimates. In our new paper, ProbabilityBench, we introduce a benchmark where the true probabilities are known exactly. We design simulated worlds with full knowledge of the data- and label-generating processes, allowing us to compute the exact class probabilities for each instance. Models must infer these probabilities from natural-language descriptions without access to the underlying generating processes. This allows us to directly measure how close their predictions are to the ground-truth probabilities. We evaluate 16 models, including decision models such as Jev and Perplexity Decider, and find that decision models often achieve strong trade-offs between probability accuracy and cost. We also show how ProbabilityBench can help evaluate existing evaluation methods, including calibration metrics and Bayes-error estimators. Until now, evaluating predictions against exact class probabilities has often meant relying on simple synthetic settings like Gaussian distributions. If you've ever wished for something more realistic and interesting, we hope you'll give ProbabilityBench a try!

title: Scaling Online Optimal Transport Minibatches for Flow Matching

details.title: Scaling Online Optimal Transport Minibatches for Flow Matching
details.abstract: A central challenge in scaling flow models is maintaining stability in training and integration. In flow matching, this stability depends critically on how source samples are paired with data. Independent random pairing introduces substantial stochasticity, motivating minibatch optimal transport (OT) to construct online source-target couplings that reduce this randomness (Tong et al., 2024). However, as applications extend to larger and higher-dimensional datasets, small minibatches can limit these benefits, while scaling the coupling to substantially larger minibatches at every iteration is computationally prohibitive. Moreover, how OT coupling affects the full stochastic gradient and integration remains theoretically unresolved. In this work, we develop a scalable online entropic OT approximation that enables substantially larger source-target couplings while preserving the benefits of OT. We close the theoretical gap for both unregularized and entropic OT by proving strict reductions in full stochastic-gradient variance and integration error relative to independent pairing, and further characterize how these improvements strengthen as the online coupling minibatch grows. Experiments on single-cell gene interpolation-flow and image-flow training validate these predictions, showing that larger online couplings consistently improve training stability and final generation performance.

title: NavGPT-3: Harnessing Context in a Hierarchical Navigation Runtime

details.title: NavGPT-3: Harnessing Context in a Hierarchical Navigation Runtime
details.abstract: Language models trained with long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning can generalize knowledge through reasoning, express precise actions, and pursue goals over many steps, raising the ceiling on what an embodied agent can understand and decide. Physical interaction, however, remains the domain of action policies, which provide dense, low-latency control. We present NavGPT-3, a harness that connects the two models, with an OS-like runtime built above it: reasoning, acting, and monitoring run as threads with their own context, tools, and permissions, while the runtime schedules them and decides which thread controls the robot's motion, so that the robot can react to sudden real-world events through interruption and thread switching. Beneath it, our action policy NavGPT VLA, trained on 19.28M examples, allocates visual tokens using codec allocation, in proportion to scene change; its 8B model alone reaches 76.94 SR on R2R-CE and leads RxR-CE with 82.39 SR. With the complete harness, NavGPT-3 sets the state of the art on R2R-CE (81.51 SR) and, for the first time, brings an autonomous agent to human level: on RxR-CE it matches human followers in success (90.43 vs. 90.4 SR) and path fidelity (78.47 vs. 77.7 nDTW) at 1 min 22 s per episode, versus roughly 3 min for a human. We comprehensively ablate the harness design and the interaction between the two models, showing how tools and the action policy shape the path from language-model reasoning to physical control: when NavGPT VLA executes the route, the reasoning loop shortens and the system's minimum reaction time falls from 3-19 s per language-model decision to 0.5-1 s per action-policy step (1-2 Hz). These results show that designing this embodied interface is central to connecting frontier language-model intelligence with low-level physical control. We will release all models, code, and evaluation records.

title: SWEeper-Bench: Can Agents Discover Bugs in Interactive Software?

details.title: SWEeper-Bench: Can Agents Discover Bugs in Interactive Software?
details.abstract: SWEeper-Bench tests whether coding agents can find and fix bugs that nobody has reported yet. It has 200 tasks, each built from a real bug fix in a different open-source web app. The agent gets the codebase and an open-ended request such as "Find and fix issues in SearXNG's search suggestion interface." It is not told what the bug is. The bugs only appear after a sequence of normal user actions, so the agent has to run the app and test it. An agentic verifier then checks the patch in a browser, the way a user would. The best of 15 frontier agents passes 59.0% of tasks. Building is half the loop. Sweeping is the other. Visit https://sweeperbench.com for the gap. 🧹

title: MimicX: Policy-in-the-Loop Supervision Refinement for Video-Driven Humanoid Motion Tracking

details.title: MimicX: Policy-in-the-Loop Supervision Refinement for Video-Driven Humanoid Motion Tracking
details.abstract: 🚀 MimicX: Turning Execution Failures into Better Humanoid Learning A human video shows what a motion should look like. A physics-based rollout reveals what a robot still needs to learn. MimicX connects the two. Rather than repeatedly training against unchanged supervision, MimicX uses the robot's own execution feedback to decide where to focus, what to refine, and which updates to keep . 🔁 From failure to refinement Diagnose: locate difficult transitions and body-specific tracking errors in policy rollouts. Refine: adapt task-aware tracking objectives and training curricula, then continue policy learning. Verify: retain improvements through repeated execution checks, not higher training rewards alone. 📊 Better tracking. Longer execution. Across four video-driven humanoid tasks, our controlled experiments show 25.7% lower body-tracking error and 255.6% longer Robust Execution Horizons , averaged across tasks relative to Fixed Reference training. Further studies cover additional motions and collision-rich environments. MimicX-HLoop overlaps GPU rollout and CPU diagnosis to accelerate feedback while preserving refinement decisions. 🎬 Four skills, five synchronized views The video brings together Tennis Swing, Football Juggling, Dance Sequence, and Kung Fu , each showing the human input alongside Fixed Reference, BeyondMimic, SONIC, and MimicX. These are the latest selected website recordings; the numerical results above come from the paper's controlled study. Explore MimicX 🎬 Project page & videos · 📄 Paper 💻 Code · 🤗 Pretrained policies · 📦 Motion assets & data Code, checkpoints, motion assets, and reproduction instructions are public. We'd love to hear which skills you would like to see this loop tackle next.

title: Diff Diffusion: Predicting Edit Paths with Diffusion Models for Efficient Code Editing

details.title: Diff Diffusion: Predicting Edit Paths with Diffusion Models for Efficient Code Editing
details.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are appealing for code generation because they can update many tokens in parallel, yet many are optimized for sequence synthesis rather than edit prediction. This setting is poorly matched to modern AI-assisted IDEs, where edit prediction must infer the next code change from recent edits, the current file, and cursor-local context. Such changes are usually sparse and preserve most source tokens, so regenerating a full code segment wastes computation. We propose Diff Diffusion, a diffusion-inspired LLM framework for code editing that predicts edit paths from an original snippet to its revised form. Diff Diffusion represents denoising as structured edit operations, and combines this formulation with multi-stage training and efficient parallel decoding. By focusing computation on changed regions, Diff Diffusion supports accurate low-latency edits and multi-position parallel modification. Across public edit-completion benchmarks, edit-prediction evaluations, and online validation, Diff Diffusion matches or leads autoregressive baselines while delivering 2.78 times faster inference on public edit-completion benchmarks and a 39.0% P50 model-latency reduction in production. This work provides a new modeling perspective for AI applications that require high accuracy and low latency.

title: The COUNT: Counting N-grams Unlocks Scaling on Host Memory and Training-Free Adaptation

details.title: The COUNT: Counting N-grams Unlocks Scaling on Host Memory and Training-Free Adaptation
details.abstract: COUNT adds an n-gram embedding to a transformer without adding learned parameters. At each position, it looks up the most frequent next tokens in a table of corpus n-gram counts held in CPU RAM, and adds the model’s own output-head rows for those tokens to the token embedding. Because the table lives in host memory rather than on the GPU, it can grow to hundreds of GB, and swapping in a table counted on a new domain (math, biomedical, law) adapts a trained model with no further training. With a 1B backbone COUNT matches a standard transformer trained with 57% more compute. We release the n-gram tables (17 GB to 797 GB, plus the three domain tables), and the checkpoints for COUNT and both baselines at 7 sizes from 60M to 1B parameters: https://huggingface.co/collections/IanMagnusson/count

title: Training LLMs for Multi-Agent Collaboration with Verifiable Information Rewards

details.title: Training LLMs for Multi-Agent Collaboration with Verifiable Information Rewards
details.abstract: 🚀 Can we train LLMs to collaborate, rather than only design better multi-agent workflows? I'm sharing our new preprint, Training LLMs for Multi-Agent Collaboration with Verifiable Information Rewards (CoSIR). Most LLM post-training focuses on chatbots and individual agents: instruction following, reasoning, and task completion. In multi-agent systems (MAS), however, connecting several LLMs through prompts or workflows does not guarantee effective teamwork. Agents need to learn when to share useful evidence, when to ask teammates for missing information, and how to incorporate their contributions into decisions. So we ask: can collaboration itself be an explicit target of LLM post-training? 💡 The challenge is reward design. In natural-language tasks, final success tells us little about which messages helped. A statement's value depends on what teammates already know and whether it helps them identify the correct answer. We introduce CoSIR with three components: 🔹 Scalable, verifiable environment. Agents see different parts of a rating table and must exchange information to select the best option. We can generate many tasks while tracking each agent's information and the correct answer. 🔹 Verifiable information rewards. A Bayesian evaluator scores shared evidence by its reduction in team surprisal. Requests are scored by the potential value of truthful answers, with additional rewards for correctly using received information. 🔹 Self-play RL. These fine-grained rewards directly post-train the underlying LLM, rather than only modifying an inference-time workflow. 📊 The key test is transfer to more complex tasks—not performance on the toy task alone. We post-train Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-3-4B-it, then evaluate them on 7 unseen natural-language collaboration benchmarks spanning distributed evidence, mathematical reasoning, and collaborative decision-making. CoSIR achieves the highest seven-task score sum among compared methods on all 3 backbones (Qwen3-8B: +31.85 points versus base). We also examine behavior. For Qwen3-8B on HiddenBench, private-fact disclosure rises from 68.5% to 74.3%. In MAST-based analysis pooled across the three models, failures to use teammates' input fall from 26.3% to 22.8%, and failures to seek clarification from 36.4% to 32.0%. Performance on GSM8K, MMLU, and IFEval remains largely preserved. 🎯 Our takeaway: Collaboration is a capability that should be explicitly trained. Better workflows matter—but so does teaching the underlying LLM how to work with other agents. 📄 https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17893

title: StreamErase: Towards Ultra-Fast Streaming Video Erasing

details.title: StreamErase: Towards Ultra-Fast Streaming Video Erasing
details.abstract: We progressively transfer the erasing capability from a powerful bidirectional foundation model to an efficient unidirectional streaming eraser, enabling long-horizon erasing without sacrificing visual fidelity.

title: AgentSafeEvo: Adversarial Co-Evolution for LLM Agent Safety

details.title: AgentSafeEvo: Adversarial Co-Evolution for LLM Agent Safety
details.abstract: Hi, I’m one of the authors of AgentSafeEvo. We introduce an adversarial co-evolution framework that jointly trains attacker and defender LLM agents for safer multi-turn tool use. We evaluate across seven safety and capability benchmarks and release our code, models, and datasets to support further research: https://github.com/lalalamdbf/AgentSafeEvo .

title: Vela: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models with Adaptive Action Curve Parametrization

details.title: Vela: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models with Adaptive Action Curve Parametrization
details.abstract: Most vision-language-action models represent future motion as fixed-rate action chunks, tying temporal resolution and prediction horizon to a fixed output budget. This pointwise representation wastes capacity on highly correlated neighboring actions, leaves temporal continuity and smoothness to be learned implicitly, and forces a tradeoff between long-horizon coverage and the local precision required for contact-rich manipulation. To address these limitations, we introduce Vela, a vision-language-action foundation model that represents future robot behavior as continuous trajectories. Vela combines a compact spline-based action representation with motion-dependent temporal support and a shared action interface for heterogeneous embodiments, allowing a fixed output budget to adapt its temporal resolution across motions. We pretrain Vela on large-scale multi-embodiment robot data and evaluate it on LIBERO-X, EBench, and two real-world long-horizon tasks, egg-cake cooking and potato shredding, obtaining promising results across simulation and physical manipulation. These results highlight the potential of continuous action representations as a foundation for future embodied foundation models.

title: Jag: Direct Box Prediction for Efficient Visual Grounding

details.title: Jag: Direct Box Prediction for Efficient Visual Grounding
details.abstract: We introduce Jag , a 0.8B visual grounding model that predicts bounding boxes in a single forward pass, without autoregressive coordinate generation. Jag improves over its base model on all five test splits and achieves overall Acc@0.5 comparable to LocateAnything. In our single-request benchmark, it is 3.62× faster than LocateAnything and uses 73.88% less peak GPU memory . We release the model weights, training and evaluation code, and an interactive demo. 🌐 Project · 💻 Code · 🤗 Model · 🎮 Demo Try the demo and let us know what you think. Questions and feedback are welcome!

title: Generative World Simulation with DAO and JING

details.title: Generative World Simulation with DAO and JING
details.abstract: DAO (道) computes the shared world’s state and dynamics, while JING (镜) generates each observer’s first-person experience. Actions change the world; those changes shape what humans and agents experience and how they act next. This continuous loop connects perception, decision, action, and world evolution within a world that persists beyond any individual observer.

title: SyncReward: Human-Aligned Synchronization Reward for Audio-Visual Generation

details.title: SyncReward: Human-Aligned Synchronization Reward for Audio-Visual Generation
details.abstract: Recent years have witnessed rapid progress in joint audio--visual generation. However, audio--visual synchronization remains a challenge, as generated speech and sound often temporally misalign with visual events. A key bottleneck is the lack of human-annotated data, reliable evaluation benchmarks, and synchronization-aware evaluation models for generated audio--visual outputs. To address these limitations, we conduct a comprehensive study spanning data, benchmarking, and reward modeling. We first introduce SyncReward-Data-80K, a dataset containing 80K professional synchronization ratings for clips from eight audio--visual generators. A taxonomy-guided construction pipeline covers four sound-event families: Speech, Onset, Instrument, and Ambient. We further construct \textbf{SyncReward-Bench}, a held-out benchmark of 1K clips, each independently rated by multiple professionals. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate specialized synchronization metrics and omni-modal models, revealing their substantial misalignment with human judgments. Finally, we develop SyncReward, a reward model that combines semantic--temporal contrastive pretraining on real clips with human supervision on generated clips. As an evaluation metric, SyncReward achieves the strongest agreement with human ratings among the evaluated methods. As a reward, it improves synchronization through inference-time best-of-N selection and reinforcement learning based post-training.

title: G^3VLA: Geometric Inductive Bias for Vision-Language-Action Models

details.title: G^3VLA: Geometric Inductive Bias for Vision-Language-Action Models
details.abstract: We introduce G³VLA, a camera-aware module that helps pretrained VLAs use the geometric relationships between multiple camera views. It combines intrinsic-conditioned ray embeddings, projective positional encoding, and bidirectional cross-view fusion while preserving the policy’s action space and native imitation objective. Geometry supervision can come from ground-truth point maps or an offline π³X teacher; inference requires no depth sensor or geometry teacher. The results highlight both the value of calibrated geometry and its dependence on supervision quality and the pathway connecting visual tokens to actions. We welcome discussion on integrating geometric priors into generalist robot policies!

title: MA-Bench: Measuring Operational Planning in Language Models

details.title: MA-Bench: Measuring Operational Planning in Language Models
